uncited: **Inputs:** Volume dataset $V$ (typically a 3D grid of voxels), camera parameters (view direction, projection type), and base plane orientation.
**Outputs:** Final rendered image on the image plane.
**Volume Data:** A 3D array of voxel values.
The algorithm assumes access to slices (2D planes) of this data.
**Intermediate Image Buffer:** A 2D array storing the rendered pixels for the base plane.
**Warping Parameters:** Affine transformation matrices (shear, scale, rotation) derived from the camera view relative to the volume axes.
**Base Plane Selection:** Identify the volume face (slice direction) most parallel and nearest to the image plane.

**Volume Transformation (Shear/Scale):** Transform the volume into an intermediate coordinate system such that the view direction aligns with one of the principal axes (typically the z-axis of the base plane).
This step corrects for the angle between the base plane and the image plane.
*   **Shear/Scale Factors:** Determined by the angle between the view direction and the volume axes.
*   **Base Plane Resolution:** Matches the intermediate image resolution, which may differ from the final image resolution depending on the warping step.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot M)$, where $N$ is the number of pixels in the intermediate image and $M$ is the average ray length through the volume.
The warping step adds $O(P)$, where $P$ is the number of pixels in the final image.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(V)$ for the volume data, plus $O(N)$ for the intermediate image buffer.
Hybrid Ray-Casting, also known as Template-Based Raycasting or Shear-Warp, was developed to address the inefficiencies of image-order ray casting on parallel hardware.
